title: Newt Kash Hollow (15Mf1)
summary: In Menifee County, Newt Kash rockshelter preserved Early Woodland plant remains, some of the earliest clear domesticated crops from a Kentucky shelter.
bodyMarkdown:
Newt Kash Hollow Shelter is a sandstone rockshelter in Menifee County, in eastern Kentucky. Dry deposits under its overhang preserved plant remains that rarely survive in open-air sites. Those remains made the shelter one of the key sites in the study of early plant cultivation in eastern North America.

## Seeds from the 1930s

The shelter was excavated in the 1930s, a decade of large-scale archaeology in Kentucky. The very [idea](https://grokipedia.com/page/Eastern_Agricultural_Complex) of an eastern farming complex drew on Volney H. Jones's study of plant remains from the shelter in that decade. His analysis revealed evidence of native seed processing and possible early cultivation.

The complex refers to plants that Native peoples tended long before maize became a staple. Its crops [included goosefoot](https://grokipedia.com/page/Eastern_Agricultural_Complex) (chenopod), sunflower, maygrass and erect knotweed. Over generations they were selected for larger seeds and for seed heads that held together at harvest.

## How old the crops are

Later dating pushed the story further back. A [Cambridge abstract on domesticated Chenopodium](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/american-antiquity/article/abs/domesticated-chenopodium-in-prehistoric-eastern-north-america-new-accelerator-dates-from-eastern-kentucky/B3DF657F64BE25778F511C7C225E366B) reports accelerator dates on dried goosefoot seeds from Newt Kash and [Cloudsplitter Rockshelter](/stories/cloudsplitter-rockshelter-menifee-county/), also in Menifee County. Newt Kash dated to 3400 ± 150 years before present. The authors say this extended the known age of the domesticated plant by about 1,000 years.

Newt Kash is [among](https://grokipedia.com/page/Red_River_Gorge) eastern Kentucky's main Woodland-era shelters. Their deposits include pottery, cordage, textiles, storage pits and carbonized seeds.

## A place for women?

Newer work asks what the shelter was used for. A 2011 article, [“Rock Shelters as Women's Retreats: Understanding Newt Kash,”](https://doi.org/10.7183/0002-7316.76.4.628) looks at the whole collection rather than the seeds alone. It notes abundant fibers and bedding, nuts, a cradleboard, a bedrock mortar, shell spoons and many plants with possible medicinal uses.

Animal bones were scarce, and the pits followed a pattern. From this the article proposes that Newt Kash may have been a retreat for women during menstruation, childbirth and sickness, and possibly a meeting place for a medicine society. The article treats this as one interpretation and notes possible retreat shelters elsewhere.

## Kentucky today

Newt Kash's seeds remain a reference point in studies of the Eastern Agricultural Complex, which is [among the world's independent](https://grokipedia.com/page/Eastern_Agricultural_Complex) centers of plant domestication. Forest Service surveys in the region [favor non-invasive methods](https://grokipedia.com/page/Red_River_Gorge) because looting threatens the intact layers in shelters like this one.
